#### ccf.graph.protocols.WriterLease

- Surface: ccf.graph.protocols.WriterLease
- Public surface: true
- Change type: added
- Before: absent. Nothing represented a writer's hold on its graph beyond this process's live-writer table.
- After: a Protocol for a held writer lease. It has `scope` (a `WriterLeaseScope`), `mechanism` (the lease kind and resource, credential-free), an idempotent `release()`, and context-manager entry and exit.
- Why: SEC-013. The mint holds the lease for the writer's life and gives it back on `BaseGraphWriter.close` or on boot's failure path.
- Migration: none for a deployment. An adapter author returns one from `writer_lease()`.

*Recorded by `372-13-sec-013-writer-lease.md`.*

#### ccf.graph.protocols.WriterLeaseScope

- Surface: ccf.graph.protocols.WriterLeaseScope
- Public surface: true
- Change type: added
- Before: absent.
- After: `Literal["cross-process", "process"]`. `"cross-process"` means the substrate refuses a second holder in any process. `"process"` is a disclosure, not enforcement: the only exclusion is this process's live-writer table.
- Why: SEC-013. Each lease names its own scope, so nobody has to infer whether cross-process exclusion holds.
- Migration: none.

*Recorded by `372-13-sec-013-writer-lease.md`.*

#### ccf.graph.protocols.WRITER_LEASE_SCOPES

- Surface: ccf.graph.protocols.WRITER_LEASE_SCOPES
- Public surface: true
- Change type: added
- Before: absent.
- After: the two `WriterLeaseScope` values as a tuple. The mint refuses a lease that declares anything else, with a `TypeError`.
- Why: SEC-013. The vocabulary is closed and checked at the mint.
- Migration: none.

*Recorded by `372-13-sec-013-writer-lease.md`.*

#### ccf.graph.protocols.WriterLeaseHeld

- Surface: ccf.graph.protocols.WriterLeaseHeld
- Public surface: true
- Change type: added
- Before: absent.
- After: a `RuntimeError` a store's `writer_lease()` raises when another holder has the lease. The mint turns it into the same `SingleWriterViolation` ("already exists") that an in-process second boot raises, naming the lease it could not take.
- Why: SEC-013. A backend store may not import `ccf.graph._writer` (CINV-02), so the store needs its own type for refusing.
- Migration: none for a deployment. A deployment that catches `SingleWriterViolation` at boot now also sees the cross-process refusal there.

*Recorded by `372-13-sec-013-writer-lease.md`.*

#### ccf.graph.protocols.ProcessScopedWriterLease

- Surface: ccf.graph.protocols.ProcessScopedWriterLease
- Public surface: true
- Change type: added
- Before: absent.
- After: the `"process"`-scope lease, `ProcessScopedWriterLease(*, substrate)`. Acquiring and releasing it do nothing. The memory, fluree, mongo and neo4j reference stores and the demo fixture return it.
- Why: SEC-013. This is a disclosure, not enforcement. On the persistent network stores the single-writer invariant is NOT enforced across processes, and SEC-013 stays open for them. A native lease for mongo (a lease document under a unique index) and neo4j (a unique lock node) is an executor proposal, unapproved (SEC-013-P1). Fluree is append-only and has no native lock, so what the invariant means on a shared ledger needs a ruling.
- Migration: an out-of-tree adapter with no cross-process lock returns `ProcessScopedWriterLease(substrate="<adapter name>")` from `writer_lease()`.

*Recorded by `372-13-sec-013-writer-lease.md`.*

#### ccf.controlplane.audit.AttributeAssertionRefusedAuditEvent

- Surface: ccf.controlplane.audit.AttributeAssertionRefusedAuditEvent
- Public surface: true
- Change type: added
- Before: absent.
- After: a derived `AuditEvent` with `refused_entity_class`, `refused_attribute`, `refused_source_system_id`, `refused_envelope_id` and `refused_value_present`. Each field is hash-transparent at `None`. `AuditLog.append` builds this event when it receives `refused_attribute`. The refused value is never recorded (SEC-024 discipline).
- Why: an examiner can ask which source tried to relabel which entity, without the audit plane holding a copy of the data the label protects.
- Migration: none.

#### ccf.deployment.manifest.UngovernedClassificationAttribute

- Surface: ccf.deployment.manifest.UngovernedClassificationAttribute
- Public surface: true
- Change type: added
- Before: absent. A deployment could admit on an attribute that any source could relabel.
- After: a `ValueError` subclass carrying `operator_key`, `entity_class` and `attribute`. `_register_and_boot` raises it before anything is registered, which covers both `load_and_boot` and `load_config_and_boot`. It is raised when a `PolicyFilterParametersArtifact` names `classification_attribute_by_class: {class: attribute}` and the resolution spec in force has a rule of that class that writes the attribute without `attribute_authorities` for it. A class that no rule writes the attribute for is not refused. Nothing source-asserts that attribute, and `PolicyFilter` admits such an entity to nobody.
- Why: SEC-023, Dave's correction of 2026-10-06. The L2 refusal governs only what a deployment declares. This check makes the declaration mandatory wherever classification controls access.
- Migration: a deployment whose `PolicyFilter` names a classification attribute declares `attribute_authorities` for it on every rule that writes it. Every shipped example config and the banking fixtures were updated. A fabric composed by hand through `ccf.boot.boot` never sees operator parameters, so this check does not cover it (the low road, `D-IMPL-364`).

*Recorded by `372-23-sec-023-classification-authority.md`.*

#### ccf.authz.capability.ArtifactErase

- Public surface: true

- Before: absent
- After: the erasure door's `ActionKind`. A door mints it with `mint` from an authorizer's allow. It is never composition-mintable. `ErasureDoor.request` and `ErasureDoor.complete` take it as a required keyword (`erase=`), alongside the recorded human approval. A general `Execute`/`Resume` passed in its place, or an erase capability issued for a different request, is refused by `verify` as `CapabilityBypassError`.
- Why: SEC-009; ruling 3. A principal that holds only general workflow `Execute`/`Resume` must not be able to have an erasure written.
- Migration: callers of the erasure door pass `erase=` with a capability for exactly the request.

#### ccf.replay.engine.ErasedReplayOutcome

- Surface: ccf.replay.engine.ErasedReplayOutcome
- Public surface: true
- Change type: added
- Before: absent
- After: A positive replay outcome for a replay that met erased content it would have to read to re-execute: the decision record itself, an admitted child contract, or a re-execution artifact. It carries `record_content_address`, `record` (`None` when the record itself was erased) and a non-empty `erased_content`. No product is reproduced.
- Why: SEC-009; ruling 4 (design §5.2). Replay stays positive and discloses the erasure for every erased input class. It never refuses by name, and it never re-derives a product from bytes the fabric refuses to serve.

### Not public Python API

#### tools.lints.hash_transparent_key (CINV-06)

- Surface: tools/lints/hash_transparent_key.py
- Public surface: false
- Change type: added
- Before: absent — a sentinel-defaulted field could ship without declaring its hash posture and every hash it touched would move with nothing red
- After: a whole-tree AST checker over `src/` and `runtime/`, rule id `cinv06-hash-transparent-key` (CINV-05 is reserved by `D-GATE-15.4` ruling (3) for the deferred substrate-name split), **registered under `python -m tools.lints --all` as `hash-transparent-key`** (`make lint`, the CI lint job): every defaulted field on a `CCFContract` subclass — bases closed by simple name across files — that is NOT in the base roster below must declare `ccf_hash_transparent` as the literal `True` or `False`; a missing key, a non-boolean value, or a `json_schema_extra` it cannot read statically is one finding naming `Class.field`. The universe is NEW-SINCE-`13bd250` only (amendment 2): a field in the base roster is silent whatever it declares, because its default has rendered into every hash since it shipped and its absence from a stored object is the `D-IMPL-89` lineage by construction. No allowlist and no name list of its own — the fifteen fields amendment 1 named left this module entirely and are in the roster like every other pre-phase field; as a roster they live on the replay check only (`tests/replay/test_generation_mismatch.py::THE_FIFTEEN`, the record's shape). No `allowlist.yaml` entry (`D-13`). Its first roster-bounded sweep named exactly the seven declarations amendment 2 ticks, which are now marked; the tree is clean
- Why: amendment 1 — "A forgotten key is red, not a quiet upgrade."; amendment 2 — "New-since-13bd250 only. Do not allowlist 115 names. … Base roster is a committed file measured at `13bd250`, not a comment."
- Migration: an adopter adding a sentinel-defaulted field to any `CCFContract` in `src/` or `runtime/` declares the key, or `make lint` is red naming the field. Nothing for a reader of the SDK

*Recorded by `24.5-fix-01-hash-transparency.md`.*

#### tools.lints.base_roster and tools/lints/hash_transparent_base_roster.json (the CINV-06 base roster)

- Surface: tools/lints/base_roster.py
- Public surface: false
- Change type: added
- Before: absent — "new since the phase base" had no measured boundary, so a lint over sentinel-defaulted fields either allowlisted 130 names by hand or named every one of them
- After: a committed JSON roster of every defaulted `CCFContract` field at `13bd250` — 130 names, `module.Class.field`, sorted, with a header naming the base commit (`13bd250e7a9d9ea12daf596ef86597557aad702f`), the generator and the rule — produced by `python -m tools.lints.base_roster`, which exports `src/` and `runtime/` at that commit with `git archive` and walks them with the lint's own `defaulted_fields` walker; `--check` regenerates into memory and diffs, exit 1 on drift, and fails loudly (never a clean result) when the commit is not in the clone. JSON over YAML because the lint package is stdlib-only, `json.dumps(sort_keys=True, indent=2)` is byte-deterministic so `--check` is a byte equality, and the header carries what a comment would. The CI lint job now checks out with `fetch-depth: 0` so `tools/lints/tests/test_base_roster.py` can run `--check` there
- Why: amendment 2 — the roster does not rot because nothing is ever added to it by hand; it is a measurement of one immutable tree, and `--check` proves the file is that measurement
- Migration: none. The roster is regenerated only by a ruling that moves the base; a later phase's new fields are in the lint's universe forever

*Recorded by `24.5-fix-01-hash-transparency.md`.*

#### docs/schemas/

- Surface: docs/schemas/
- Public surface: false
- Change type: added
- Before: absent — an adopter authoring an artifact document had no schema
  to point an editor at, and marshalling errors surfaced at boot
- After: one committed JSON Schema per entry in `SDK_ARTIFACT_CLASSES`
  (eleven today), each annotated `x-ccf-class-id`, regenerated by
  `make schemas` and held to the live models by a bytes-equality gate in the
  always-on `test` job that fails on drifted, missing, **and orphaned** files
- Why: D-11's generate-at-build posture has one standing exception, D-12's
  committed `openapi.json`, for contracts external consumers read. The
  schemas are the same case one step earlier: they are what adopters author
  *against*, in an editor, before anything runs, and a schema that exists
  only at build time cannot be the target of a `$schema` header in a
  checked-in document. Classes the SDK does not own get no committed schema
  — the SDK never invents one for a namespace that is not its own.
- Migration: run `make schemas` after adding or changing an `ArtifactClass`;
  a stale tree is a red build, not a silent difference

*Recorded by `15-12-schema-export.md`.*

#### make schema-headers

- Surface: make schema-headers
- Public surface: false
- Change type: added
- Before: absent — nothing checked that a `$schema` header was *correct*
- After: `tools/check_schema_headers.py` verifies, per artifact document,
  that the header resolves from the document's **own directory** (as an
  editor resolves it, not as a repo-root-relative test would), that the
  target is a committed schema annotated with a real SDK class id matching
  its file name, that the named class's contract **actually accepts the
  document**, and that any deployment manifest in the directory declares the
  same `class_id` the header names. Auto-arming: a directory joins the
  checked set as soon as it carries its first header, so each example-rewrite
  plan gates its own headers at its own wave. `DIR=<path>` narrows it;
  `--require-all` is the tree-wide form for the phase close.
- Why: an editor hint has a failure mode no runtime has — it can be wrong for
  months and nothing breaks, because nothing reads it but the adopter's
  editor, which will happily annotate a document with confident nonsense from
  a real schema for the wrong class. Existence of the target is therefore not
  the property worth gating; correctness is. Validating through the SDK's own
  `load_artifact` makes the check exactly as strong as the validator the
  adopter's fabric runs at boot, and costs no new dependency.
- Migration: run `make schema-headers DIR=<your artifacts dir>` when adding
  headers

*Recorded by `15-12-schema-export.md`.*

#### examples/00-quickstart/artifacts/

- Surface: examples/00-quickstart/artifacts/
- Public surface: false
- Change type: added
- Before: no schema annotation of any kind
- After: each document carries an explicit
  `# ccf-schema: deferred(15-13) …` first line
- Why: **no SDK artifact class accepts any of these four documents today** —
  verified, not assumed — because each is a multi-artifact bundle and the
  contracts are `extra=forbid`. A `$schema` header on such a file would
  annotate every key belonging to the other artifacts as an error, so the
  "hint" would be a wall of false positives in the adopter's editor: worse
  than no header. Plan 15-13 splits these into typed per-class documents with
  a manifest and writes the real headers then, which is also when they become
  reviewable alongside the reshaped documents. The deferral is explicit,
  greppable, names the plan that closes it, and is *counted* — a document with
  neither a header nor a marker fails the gate, so nothing falls through
  silently.
- Migration: none — the markers disappear at 15-13

*Recorded by `15-12-schema-export.md`.*

## Reshaped

Surfaces that still exist under the same name but whose shape moved. These are the entries an existing integration must read.

546 entries — 355 public Python surface, 191 not public Python API.

### Public Python surface

#### ccf.hitl.transport.HitlPolicy

- Surface: ccf.hitl.transport.HitlPolicy
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: `{semver, signed_binding_required: bool = False}`
- After: three members join, each `None` by default and hash-transparent at `None` (CINV-06): `signature_max_age_seconds: int | None` (positive), `permitted_clock_skew_seconds: int | None` (non-negative) and `trusted_keys: Mapping[str, Mapping[str, JsonWebKey]] | None` (approver subject → `kid` → public JWK). A model validator refuses `signed_binding_required: true` without all three at parse (`ArtifactLoadError` through the Control Plane), so a required policy never admits under an invented window. Two helpers: `keys_for(subject_id)` and `pinned_ref(key=, version=) -> "key@version"`
- Why: `D-IMPL-363` E3 / E5 / C6(a) — the window and the trust map are the deployment's statements in the pinned artifact (CINV-01), the ONE trust source; a second source is the hole this wave closes
- Migration: every `ccf.hitl-policy` document that sets `signed_binding_required: true` must now also state `signature_max_age_seconds`, `permitted_clock_skew_seconds` and `trusted_keys`; a document that does not is refused when registered. A policy that does not require signing is unchanged, and keeps its content address

*Recorded by `005-the-signed-claim-set-and-the-time-window.md`.*

#### ccf.hitl.transport.HitlActionRequest

- Surface: ccf.hitl.transport.HitlActionRequest
- Public surface: true

- Before: `{event_key, action, product_content_hash, annotation, signed_binding: SignedPrincipalBinding | None}`
- After: `signed_binding` is replaced by `attestation: SignedHitlAction | None` (hash-transparent at `None`). `extra=forbid` makes a body that still sends `signed_binding` a boundary refusal
- Why: `D-IMPL-363` E1 / C12(a) — the request carries the signer's own statement, in one shape at both doors

#### ccf.hitl.transport.HitlActionSubmission

- Surface: ccf.hitl.transport.HitlActionSubmission

#### ccf.hitl.transport.InMemoryHitlTransport

- Surface: ccf.hitl.transport.InMemoryHitlTransport
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: `__init__(*, control_plane=None, hitl_policy_key=None, identity_provider=None, trusted_keys=None)`; `submit` verified the signed binding against `trusted_keys`
- After: `__init__(*, control_plane=None, hitl_policy_key=None, identity_provider=None)` — no `trusted_keys`. `submit` resolves the policy, stamps `hitl_policy_ref`, runs `enforce_attestation` outside the lock when the policy requires it, and then — inside the lock, after verification and before recording — checks and inserts the nonce in one step, refusing a reuse as `SignedBindingStaleRefused`. Two racing presentations of one attestation cannot both pass
- Why: `D-IMPL-363` C6(a) (one trust source) and E4 / C11(a) (atomic nonce)
- Migration: remove the `trusted_keys=` argument; declare the keys per subject in the pinned policy instead

#### ccf.hitl.principal.HumanPrincipalBinding

- Surface: ccf.hitl.principal.HumanPrincipalBinding
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: four required fields — `approver`, `authentication`, `action_time`,
  `product_content_hash`. The verdict was not among them, so
  `canonical_bytes(binding)` did not cover it and
  `ccf.hitl.transport.enforce_signed_binding` compared only the signature and
  the principal
- After: a fifth required field, `verdict: str`, marked
  `json_schema_extra={HASH_TRANSPARENT_KEY: False}` — a `D-IMPL-243`
  generation boundary, rendered into every binding's hash, so a stored object
  lacking it is named by `generation_mismatch` rather than verifying
  silently. `enforce_signed_binding` now raises `SignedBindingInvalidRefused`
  when the verified binding's `verdict` is not the submission's `action`
- Why: a signature that still verifies after the action is swapped authorizes
  a decision the approver never made (`SEC-005`). Binding the verdict into the
  signed bytes is what makes non-repudiation mean what a deployment that
  turned `HitlPolicy.signed_binding_required` on already believed it meant
- Migration: **a client that signs its own binding must include the verdict,
  and it must equal the action the client submits.** The served doors need no
  change — both mint the binding through
  `ccf_runtime.identity_binding.principal_from_authorized`, which binds the
  verdict from the request field the submission already carries. For
  `ccf.hitl.override.OverrideBoundary` the submitted action is derived
  (`override` when a substitute is supplied, otherwise `approve`), so an
  approver signs the verdict matching the resolve they are performing. The
  binding's content hash moves for every instance, by design; no stored signed
  binding is re-verified anywhere in the SDK, so nothing written before this
  change has to keep verifying

#### ccf.assembly.worker.IdentityRefused

- Surface: ccf.assembly.worker.IdentityRefused
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: `__init__(*, envelope_id: str, entity_class: str, key: str,
  field: str, reason: str)` — every field required; `reason ∈ {"null",
  "empty", "bool", "float", "non-finite", "non-scalar"}`, all of them faults
  of a VALUE on a declared identity key. A rule declaring zero identity keys
  was refused at the same mint site as a bare `ValueError`, outside this class
- After: `__init__(*, envelope_id: str, entity_class: str, reason: str,
  key: str | None = None, field: str | None = None)`. A seventh reason,
  `undeclared`, names an EMPTY DECLARATION: a matching rule with
  `identity_keys == ()` raises `IdentityRefused(envelope_id=…,
  entity_class=…, reason="undeclared")` with `key is None` and
  `field is None`, because nothing was read and there is no key or field to
  name, and its message reads *"envelope … matched rule for …, which declares
  no identity keys (undeclared); the fabric refuses to mint a URI from empty
  identity (SEC-007)"*. The six value reasons keep `key` and `field` set and
  their message unchanged
- Why: `IdentityRefused` is the SDK-owned seam class the governed path
  converts by mechanism (`SDK_SEAM_REFUSALS`, unchanged), so raising the
  empty-declaration fault BY NAME is what turns a traceback with no record
  into a refusal at the `acquisition` seam whose replay record carries
  `identity-refused` / `nonexistent` and the worker's own detail. The map is
  not widened and the product class declares nothing: the conversion is the
  existing one
- Migration: none for a caller constructing the class — `key` and `field`
  are keyword-only and still accepted, so every existing construction site is
  unchanged. A caller that catches `IdentityRefused` and reads `key` or
  `field` must now accept `None` for the `undeclared` reason. A deployment
  whose resolution spec declares a rule with `identity_keys: []` now receives
  a governed refusal on the paved road where it previously received a
  traceback; the declaration itself still constructs, by ruling, so the
  refusal can name the envelope that reached the mint

*Recorded by `007-empty-identity-declaration-refused-by-name.md`.*

#### ccf.workflow.definitions.WorkflowDefinition

- Surface: ccf.workflow.definitions.WorkflowDefinition
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: no field declared which verdict at a gate leads to which
  transition target. A `WorkflowDefinition` could route a `hitl-gate`-kind
  step's approving and rejecting branches from nothing more than whatever
  decision string an engine happened to read at resume time.
- After: a new field, `gate_routes: Mapping[str, Mapping[str, str]]` (gate
  step name → verdict → declared target), default `{}`. A
  `model_validator(mode="after")` refuses: a route key naming no
  non-terminal node in the wrapper's declared transition graph; a verdict
  outside `GATE_ACTIONS` (`ccf.hitl.approval_gate`,
  `frozenset({"approve", "reject"})`); a route target that is not a
  declared outgoing transition target from that gate; and two verdicts from
  one gate naming the same target (a map that would let a recorded
  rejection resolve identically to an approval). The field is marked
  `ccf_hash_transparent: False` (`ccf.contracts.canonical.HASH_TRANSPARENT_KEY`)
  — a declared generation boundary (`D-IMPL-243` amendment 1), not a silent
  default: a stored `WorkflowDefinition` document that predates this field
  is of an earlier generation, named by `generation_mismatch` (by field
  name, before re-execution), never silently treated as compatible. Whether
  a declared key names a `hitl-gate`-kind step is, like `gate_policies`,
  the `WorkflowFactory`'s semantic check, not this contract's.
- Why: `SEC-001` — nothing in the artifact declared which verdict goes
  where, so a recorded rejection had no declared route distinct from an
  approval's. `gate_routes` is that declared map; later tasks in this lane
  (`A2` factory-level completeness check on `hitl-gate`-kind steps, `A3`
  engine-side compare against the recorded decision, `A4` refusal of
  conflicting verdicts on one suspension) consume it by name and shape —
  neither is renamed nor reshaped here.
  **A routed gate declares at least TWO distinct outgoing transition
  targets.** It follows from the validators rather than being declared
  separately: every
  route target must be a declared transition target from that gate, two
  verdicts from one gate must not share a target, and `A2`'s factory check
  requires a target for every `GATE_ACTIONS` verdict. A gate with a single
  outgoing edge satisfies no pair of those, so a workflow that relied on
  `D-IMPL-61` propagate-to-terminal for its rejecting branch — as the
  covenant fixture's own comment does for exception refs
  (`tests/fixtures/banking/workflows/covenant_review_workflow.yaml`) — now
  declares an explicit reject edge. That is the lane's intent; what was
  missing is that an author met it as two refusals from two modules with the
  rule stated nowhere. It is now one clause on the `gate_routes` field
  docstring (`src/ccf/workflow/definitions.py`).
  **A `hitl-gate`-kind step is never a declared terminal state.** `A2`'s
  factory refuses any step whose kind in the resolved TaskDefinition is
  `hitl-gate`
  and whose name appears in `effective_terminal_states`. Review measured both
  shapes this closes: named in `terminal_states` and reached as a transition
  target, the execution COMPLETES at the gate's name with no suspension and no
  human action; as the START node, it suspends and can never resume. Neither
  was reached by the completeness check, because `routable` subtracts the
  terminal states — so "gate" silently meant two different no-ops depending on
  how it was reached. A gate is a place a human acts, never a terminal
  condition. A deployment whose workflow declares such a step is refused at
  construction, which is a behavior change to `WorkflowFactory.construct` on a
  shape that could not have worked as its author intended.
- Migration: **for THIS task alone — the contract change, before any factory
  check — none:** the field defaults to `{}`, so a `WorkflowDefinition`
  document written before it still validates. That is the extent of the
  no-migration claim, and it is scoped to A1 deliberately, because **the lane
  as a whole does require migration** and an adopter reading only this bullet
  would decide a release needs no work. In one clause: **every workflow
  document whose wrapped task declares a `hitl-gate` step the wrapper can
  reach must declare a complete `gate_routes` entry for that gate — a target
  for each of the two `GATE_ACTIONS` verdicts, hence at least two distinct
  outgoing transition targets — and must not name that gate in
  `terminal_states`.** A document that does not is refused at
  `WorkflowFactory.construct` (`A2`), and the terminal-gate refusal rejects
  shapes that previously constructed, which is the behavior change the two
  clauses above describe. **Content hashes move, by design and for every
  `WorkflowDefinition` document — not only gate-bearing ones** — because the
  field is a declared generation boundary
  (`{HASH_TRANSPARENT_KEY: False}`) rather than a silent default, so it
  renders at its default too; measured on a definition with no gate at all,
  `5f09ffe6…` → `2f507135…`, and a stored document lacking the field is named
  by `generation_mismatch` rather than run. The three in-tree gate-bearing
  documents took **one routing entry each — not one line**: each needed a
  `schema_version` bump to `2.0.0` plus a four-line `gate_routes` block, which
  measures **10, 8 and 7 changed lines** (`git diff --numstat 00fde747..HEAD`)
  for the covenant fixture, the payment-release fixture and
  `perf/synth/artifacts/workflow.yaml`. An adopter sizes work from this figure,
  so it states the entry count and the line count separately. The archived
  example transcluded by
  `public/reference/artifacts/workflow-definitions.md` declares no routes and
  would now be refused, which that page says on its face.

*Recorded by `357-A1-gate-routes.md`.*

#### ccf.products.request.ArgumentDomain

- Surface: ccf.products.request.ArgumentDomain
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: three fields — `minimum: Decimal | None`, `maximum: Decimal | None`, `members: tuple[str | int | bool | Decimal, ...] | None`; exactly one of two shapes (numeric bounds OR an enumerated set), enforced by pairwise comparison
- After: a fourth field, `pattern: str | None = None` (hash-transparent `True`), and exactly one of THREE shapes, enforced by a shape COUNT rather than a pairwise chain. A pattern is judged by `re.fullmatch` (never `re.search` — a value that merely contains the grammar satisfies a wider domain than the one declared) and is compiled once at construction so a non-compiling grammar is refused by name where the author can still fix it. `refuses(value)` returns `"not-in-domain"` for a non-string, or for a string the grammar does not match in full. **A declared grammar is additionally SHAPE-CHECKED at construction** (`D-IMPL-357` C4, round-3 ruling): a nested quantifier, an ambiguous alternation under a repeat, two unbounded repeats side by side over overlapping characters, and a repeat whose body can match nothing are each refused by name — and so is any shape the check cannot establish as safe (a backreference, a repeat inside a look-around, a conditional group, an unknown character category). The analysis is structural, over the standard library's own parse of the pattern; it adds no dependency, no timeout, no thread and no subprocess, and it never runs the pattern against text.
- Why: `D-IMPL-357` C4 — an identifier whose legal form is a RULE (an LEI, an internal account format, a jurisdiction code) cannot be declared as a roster, and the alternative an adopter reaches for is validation in deployment code, which is a second authority over one bound (`D-IMPL-315`). Sentinel-silent at `None` (`D-IMPL-243`), so every domain written before the grammar existed canonicalizes byte-for-byte as it did and no committed request contract's content address moves.
- Migration: none for any existing declaration. An author who reads the refusal message should note it now names a shape COUNT ("declares 2") rather than "both"; the word "neither" is retained for the no-shape case. **A grammar whose shape this check refuses must be simplified before it can be declared**, which is a narrowing with no shipped declaration behind it — `pattern` is introduced in this same unreleased lane, so no committed artifact is affected. The refusal is at REGISTRATION and never at serve: a caller can never trigger it.

*Recorded by `357-C4-subject-domain.md`.*

#### ccf.products.request.ProductRequestContract

- Surface: ccf.products.request.ProductRequestContract
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: no declaration surface for the subject; a class could constrain any declared parameter and nothing about the address axis the question is actually about
- After: `subject_domain: ArgumentDomain | None = None` (hash-transparent `True`), plus a validator refusing a NUMERIC subject domain by name — a subject is an identifier, not a magnitude, so bounds over one bound nothing (the sibling of the existing `unmeasurable` refusal over a declared `string`). `from_declared` reads it as the optional NINTH declaration key, so the field is reachable from an artifact and not only from Python. The declaration-time domain validator additionally refuses a `pattern` declared over a parameter whose type is not `string` (a grammar judges text; over any other type no value could satisfy it), named in the same exhaustive message as the five defects it already reports.
- Why: `D-IMPL-357` C4. An adopter who knows their subjects are LEIs should be able to say so in the governed declaration rather than nowhere. Sentinel-silent at `None`, so every request contract written before the field keeps its content address; a declared domain renders and therefore MOVES the hash, deliberately — two classes holding their subjects to different grammars must not share one contract identity.
- Migration: none. A contract declaring no `subject_domain` holds its subject to exactly what it did: the mechanism floor, judged by `refuse_floor`, which no declaration can reach under. A contract declaring one is held to the same grammar shape check as any argument domain, and additionally refuses a NON-STRING member set — `ProductRequest.subject` is typed `str`, so such a set is satisfied by no subject that could ever be presented.

*Recorded by `357-C4-subject-domain.md`.*

#### ccf.assembly.worker.EntityResolutionSpec

- Surface: ccf.assembly.worker.EntityResolutionSpec
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: a `CCFContract` with `entity_rules` and `relationship_rules` and no
  version field of any kind
- After: inherits `ccf.controlplane.artifact_base.VersionedArtifact`; `semver`
  is required and has **no default**
- Why: D-IMPL-77. The class's own docstring already called it "a Control Plane
  artifact, versioned like any other" — the field's absence made that sentence
  aspirational, and was one of exactly three things keeping the spec away from
  the `parse_artifact` seam. A **wrapper** holding `semver` beside the spec was
  rejected: `ccf.boot.boot` would then receive a wrapper where it expects a
  spec, changing `boot()`'s signature — the one contract D-05 committed to
  preserving. The wrapper trades a data change for a contract change, which is
  the more expensive of the two. No default, because a default lane is a version
  nobody chose and the registry's D-05 bump check would then compare content
  hashes against a lane the author never asserted
- Migration: **the content hash changes.** `semver` participates in
  `content_hash(spec)`, so every `resolution_spec_version` pin minted after this
  change differs from one minted before it, and every Decision Replay record
  carrying such a pin is pinned to a new value. Existing replay records remain
  valid against the artifact versions they name — nothing is invalidated and no
  record changes shape — but a re-registration of the *same* resolution rules
  now produces a different pin than it did before. Constructing an
  `EntityResolutionSpec` without `semver` is now a validation error: state the
  lane, and prefer reading it from the artifact rather than inlining one
  (CLAUDE.md §6.4)

*Recorded by `15-07-resolution-spec.md`.*

#### ccf.controlplane.artifacts.ManifestEntry

- Surface: ccf.controlplane.artifacts.ManifestEntry
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: `path`, `key`, `class_id`, `role` — four required fields, and nothing said
  which registration path the entry travelled. `load_and_boot` called `register_typed`
  for every `role: register` entry unconditionally
- After: a fifth required field, `registration: RegistrationMode`, with **no default**
- Why: D-IMPL-85 (Dave, 2026-08-05). Either default would have the SDK deciding the
  *governance path* by silence for every entry that omitted it — a deployment would
  inherit or lose the D-05 bump check with no document saying so, which is exactly the
  convention-mistaken-for-enforcement failure this phase exists to close (T-15.1-02-01).
  The argument is a sibling of `role`'s, not a copy of it: `role`'s no-default reasoning
  is about a replay-dimension-2 *boundary*, and this one is about which governance
  obligations *run*. Rejected: optional-defaulting-to-`typed`, which is the cheap
  migration and the silent choice at once. The cost was accepted and measured with the
  ruling — 163 entries across 11 manifests plus the deployment test fixtures, one
  mechanical wave, and no external adopters to carry it (private repo, pre-1.0)
- Migration: **every manifest entry must now declare `registration`.** The mechanical
  edit is one line per entry, directly under `role`:

#### ccf.deployment.pins.ArtifactPin

- Surface: ccf.deployment.pins.ArtifactPin
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: `key`, `version`, `class_id` — the pin recorded what was in force and under
  which contract, and said nothing about how it got there
- After: a fourth required field, `registration: RegistrationMode`, carrying the mode
  the entry actually travelled
- Why: D-IMPL-83 (Dave, 2026-08-05). Bump evidence had to be reachable from the returned
  pins, and `ResolvedPins` is under an explicit no-growth constraint pinned by
  `tests/deployment/test_manifest.py::test_resolved_pins_has_exactly_one_public_method`.
  The reading adopted: that constraint forbids **methods that select**, not **fields
  that record** — `class_id` is already a recorded fact of the same kind — so the mode
  lands as a field and `ResolvedPins` gains no accessor. The audit log remains the
  **primary** evidence: `register_versioned` already audits every outcome with
  `action="register_versioned"` and `resolved=True|False`, which is how
  `test_the_author_versioned_definitions_kept_their_bump_check` reads it today. This
  field is the convenience for a reader holding the pins and no audit log. Rejected:
  audit-log-only, which leaves the evidence unreachable from the returned pins; and a
  `ResolvedPins` accessor, which contradicts the no-growth constraint directly
- Migration: **the pin set's content hash changes** — the field is additive to a
  `CCFContract`, so anything that recorded a pin-set hash before this plan records a
  different one after it. Determinism is unaffected:
  `test_two_loads_of_one_manifest_produce_an_identical_pin_set` still passes because
  both loads change identically. Code constructing an `ArtifactPin` directly must supply
  the field; code reading `version_for` is untouched

*Recorded by `15.1-02-registration-mode.md`.*

- After: `backend: Literal["sqlite", "postgres", "memory", "neo4j", "mongo",
  "fluree"]` — one new member; **no existing backend name is removed**. The
  regenerated `docs/schemas/ccf.deployment-manifest.json` enum matches. The
  field stays kind-only: no URL field, no token field, no connection value of
  any sort enters this content-hashed artifact
- Why: a declarable substrate must be declarable in the one versioned document
  that says what a deployment puts in force — and the audit plane must be able
  to answer "which substrate" without ever having stored "how to reach it"
- Migration: none for existing manifests — the Literal widened, so every
  previously valid document still validates

#### ccf.boot.boot

- Surface: ccf.boot.boot
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: sixteen keyword arguments, eleven of them per-database
  (`database_path`, `postgres_dsn`, `postgres_schema`, `memory`, `neo4j_uri`,
  `neo4j_partition`, `mongo_uri`, `mongo_partition`, `fluree_url`,
  `fluree_partition`, `fluree_bearer_token`), with the substrate selected by
  asking which of them was not `None`. Omitting all of them selected the
  development substrate by default
- After: eight keyword arguments — `backend`, `connection`, `secrets`,
  `registry`, `resolution_spec_key`, `resolution_spec_version`,
  `policy_bundle_key`, `policy_bundle_version`. `backend` is required and has
  no default; `connection` is a mapping validated against the resolved
  adapter's own contract; `secrets` is a mapping of config field to
  `ccf.graph.registry.ResolvedSecret`. No parameter names a database
- Why: the composition root named all six substrates, so adding a seventh cost
  an edit in core and a substrate name in core was unavoidable. After
  D-IMPL-93 an adapter declares itself and `boot` resolves the one a deployment
  named, which is what lets a third-party adapter ship as a separate
  installable distribution with no line changing in this repository. `backend`
  is required rather than defaulted because a fabric that could infer its own
  substrate could boot against a development store in production and still pass
  every test
- Migration: replace the per-database keyword with `backend=` plus
  `connection=`, using this table. `postgres_schema` became `schema_name`
  because a Pydantic field named `schema` shadows an attribute on `BaseModel`;
  the store's own keyword is unchanged.
  | Retired `boot()` keyword | New location |
  |---|---|
  | `database_path` | `backend="sqlite"`, `connection={"database_path": ...}` — name unchanged |
  | `postgres_dsn` | `backend="postgres"`, `connection={"dsn": ...}` |
  | `postgres_schema` | `backend="postgres"`, `connection={"schema_name": ...}` |
  | `memory=True` | `backend="memory"`, no connection mapping at all |
  | `neo4j_uri` | `backend="neo4j"`, `connection={"uri": ...}` |
  | `neo4j_partition` | `backend="neo4j"`, `connection={"partition": ...}` |
  | `mongo_uri` | `backend="mongo"`, `connection={"uri": ...}` |
  | `mongo_partition` | `backend="mongo"`, `connection={"partition": ...}` |
  | `fluree_url` | `backend="fluree"`, `connection={"url": ...}` |
  | `fluree_partition` | `backend="fluree"`, `connection={"partition": ...}` |
  | `fluree_bearer_token` | `secrets={"bearer_token": ResolvedSecret(...)}` |
  Two worked cases follow, and then the three refusals to expect while
  migrating.

*Recorded by `15.4-05-boot.md`.*

#### ccf.boot.FabricHandle

- Surface: ccf.boot.FabricHandle
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: constructed with `reader`, `worker`, `registry` and `shutdown`, and
  exposing the first three. It carried capabilities and no state a caller could
  misuse
- After: additionally constructed with `adapter` and exposing
  `handle.adapter`, a `ccf.graph.registry.AdapterPin` carrying the adapter's
  name, its version, and the sorted names of the credential references in force
- Why: from D-IMPL-93 onward the adapter behind the graph seam can be
  third-party code, so which adapter answered and at which version is part of
  what produced the answer — whitepaper §7.10.1 dimension 2. The pin has no
  field that can hold a credential: `secret_refs` carries reference *names*,
  which is what makes the credential path auditable without recording a
  credential. `FabricHandle` still has no writer attribute, private or
  otherwise
- Migration: none for a reader. A caller that constructs a `FabricHandle`
  directly — which nothing in the SDK does outside `boot` — must now pass
  `adapter`

*Recorded by `15.4-05-boot.md`.*

#### ccf.deployment.manifest.load_and_boot

- Surface: ccf.deployment.manifest.load_and_boot
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: eight keyword arguments, six of them per-database — `database_path`,
  `postgres_dsn`, `neo4j_uri`, `mongo_uri`, `fluree_url`,
  `fluree_bearer_token` — checked against a hand-maintained mapping from
  substrate name to required argument that lived in core and was edited once
  per substrate forever
- After: four — `manifest_path`, `registry`, `connection`, `tenant_id`.
  `connection` is one mapping keyed by the field names on the declared
  adapter's own connection contract, validated against it. The credential no
  longer travels as an argument at all: the manifest names it, under
  `backend_secrets`, and boot resolves the named environment variable
- Why: the manifest layer held the last two substrate enumerations in core —
  the six-name `Literal` and the required-argument table — so adding a seventh
  adapter cost an edit here. Each adapter now declares its own connection
  contract (D-07) and the registry answers which adapters a deployment has, so
  this function enumerates nothing. Two accepted costs, recorded rather than
  worked around: the exported JSON Schema loses its `backend` enum, so an
  adopter's editor no longer completes the name — plan 15.4-09's `ccf backends`
  command replaces that by answering the better question, "what is installed
  here" rather than "what did someone hard-code"; and an unknown name is now
  caught at load rather than at parse, paid back by a refusal that can list what
  *is* registered. Keeping the retired keywords as deprecated pass-throughs was
  considered and rejected: it would have left adapter names in the public
  surface indefinitely, which is what D-IMPL-93 property (2) exists to remove
- Migration: replace the per-database keyword with a `connection` mapping using
  this table, and move any credential into the manifest. A key that changed name
  and was not migrated does not read as a rename — it reads as
  `extra_forbidden` on a key you are sure exists, which is why the table is
  here rather than one fragment away.
  | Retired `load_and_boot` keyword | New location |
  |---|---|
  | `database_path` | `connection={"database_path": ...}` — name unchanged |
  | `postgres_dsn` | `connection={"dsn": ...}` |
  | `neo4j_uri` | `connection={"uri": ...}` |
  | `mongo_uri` | `connection={"uri": ...}` |
  | `fluree_url` | `connection={"url": ...}` |
  | `fluree_bearer_token` | a `backend_secrets` entry in the manifest, resolved from the environment |
  The mapping additionally reaches every other field an adapter's contract
  declares, which the old keyword list could not: `connection={"schema_name":
  ...}` where a keyword `postgres_schema` never existed here, and
  `connection={"partition": ...}` for the adapters that take one. `schema_name`
  rather than `schema` because a Pydantic field named `schema` shadows an
  attribute on `BaseModel`; the store's own keyword is unchanged.
  Before and after, for a caller with no credential:
  `load_and_boot(MANIFEST, registry=registry, database_path=str(path))` becomes
  `load_and_boot(MANIFEST, registry=registry, connection={"database_path": str(path)})`.
  For a caller with one, the argument disappears entirely: delete
  `fluree_bearer_token=os.environ["CCF_FLUREE_TOKEN"]` from the call and add
  `backend_secrets: [{field: bearer_token, env_var: CCF_FLUREE_TOKEN}]` to the
  manifest. The value still never enters the manifest and still is never
  persisted; what the manifest gains is the auditable record of *which*
  reference was in force.
  Three refusals to expect while migrating, none of which reproduces a value
  that was supplied: an adapter name nothing registers raises
  `ccf.graph.registry.UnknownBackend` listing what `declared_names()` returns; a
  connection key the adapter does not declare raises
  `ccf.graph.registry.InvalidBackendConfig` naming the adapter and the key; a
  `backend_secrets` entry whose variable is unset or empty raises `ValueError`
  naming the adapter, the field and the variable name.

*Recorded by `15.4-06-manifest.md`.*

#### ccf.controlplane.artifacts.DeploymentManifest

- Surface: ccf.controlplane.artifacts.DeploymentManifest
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: `backend` was a `Literal` over six fixed names, and a deployment's
  credentials appeared nowhere in the document
- After: `backend` is a plain `str` constrained by `^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$` — a shape
  rule, not a vocabulary — with membership checked at load against
  `ccf.graph.registry.declared_names()`. A new optional `backend_secrets` holds
  `ccf.controlplane.artifacts.SecretReference` entries, with a validator
  refusing a repeated `field`
- Why: six database names in a core contract is exactly what CLAUDE.md §11
  forbids, and generating the list rather than typing it would not have changed
  that. Which adapters exist is a property of the deployment that parses the
  document, not of the document — so the document carries the name and the
  deployment answers whether it has one. `backend_secrets` closes the other
  half: a credential must never enter a content-hashed artifact, but the
  *reference* to one can, and that is what makes "which credential was in
  force" answerable from replay for the first time
- Migration: **none — no existing manifest needs an edit**, and there is a
  mechanical reason rather than a hopeful one. Every name the retired `Literal`
  admitted is a name the pattern admits and the registry registers, so every
  manifest in the tree parses byte-unchanged. Manifests are content-addressed by
  their file bytes, so no existing replay pin moves either. What changes is what
  a manifest *may* now say: a name a third-party adapter registers, and a
  `backend_secrets` block. The committed schema at
  `docs/schemas/ccf.deployment-manifest.json` is regenerated in the same commit,
  so an adopter authoring against it sees the pattern in place of the enum and
  sees `backend_secrets` on the same day the code accepts it.

*Recorded by `15.4-06-manifest.md`.*

#### ccf.replay.record.build_replay_record

- Surface: ccf.replay.record.build_replay_record
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: ten keyword parameters; dimension 2 carried no adapter pin and the

- After: one further optional keyword, `adapter: AdapterPin | None = None`.
  Supplied, its three values land on dimension 2 with `secret_refs` sorted;
  omitted or `None`, the three positive sentinels apply and every field the
  builder wrote before this extension is byte-for-byte what it was

  and 15.2-11 extensions, because the adapter is a property of the **fabric**
  and the execution object has never seen the fabric — it carries what the
  engine ran, not what the deployment booted against. D-06 additionally keeps
  dimension-2 assembly in adopter code
- Migration: pass `adapter=booted.handle.adapter` to start pinning. Nothing is
  required of an existing caller: omitting the keyword is supported and
  records the positive `no-adapter` claim rather than falling silent

#### ccf_runtime.mcp.egress.build_egress_server

- Surface: ccf_runtime.mcp.egress.build_egress_server
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: `(*, server_name, resolver)` — the `FastMCP` constructor received
  neither `token_verifier` nor `auth`, so this door was unauthenticated, and it
  bound no authorizer of any kind
- After: four further required keyword-only parameters — `token_verifier`,
  `auth_settings`, `entitlement_source`, `perspective_resolver`. The verifier
  pair reaches the `FastMCP` constructor; the governance pair is consulted
  inside the product resource before the resolver is reached
- Why: an entitlement check downstream of no authentication asks "may this
  principal receive this class?" about a principal nobody verified, so
  authentication had to come first — and `FastMCP` installs its authentication
  middleware only at construction and only when both halves are present (D-26),
  so it cannot be retrofitted onto the returned object. The governance pair is
  required rather than optional-and-inert because this door is receiving its
  first authentication *and* its first authorization at once: `hitl.py`'s
  optional posture exists because it retrofits authorization onto a door that
  had already shipped, whereas an optional seam here would ship exactly the gap
  `docs/CONTEXT_PRODUCT_REVISION.md` §11.2 measured and would make
  deny-by-default a deployment's choice rather than the SDK's
- Migration: every existing caller breaks, and deliberately so — there is no
  configuration of this builder that answers everyone. Supply (1) a
  `TokenVerifier`: `SourceBackedTokenVerifier(source=...)` over a
  `TokenSourceProtocol`; `FileTokenSource` is the development reference and a
  production deployment substitutes its own identity infrastructure. (2) an
  `AuthSettings` carrying the deployment's issuer, resource-server identity and
  required scopes. (3) an `entitlement_source`:
  `ControlPlaneProductEntitlementSource(control_plane=..., clock=...)` over a
  registry holding a `ccf.product-entitlement-policy` registered under
  `product_entitlement_key(tenant_id=...)`. (4) a `perspective_resolver`:
  `(*, grant, tenant, requested_role) -> Perspective` deriving the role from the
  verified grant — this surface's URI has three segments and no role among
  them, so `requested_role` is always `None` here. Worked example:
  `examples/04-cross-process/producer_child.py` with
  `artifacts/egress-door.yaml`

*Recorded by `15.5-06-egress-entitlement.md`.*

#### ccf_runtime.mcp.experience.build_experience_server

- Surface: ccf_runtime.mcp.experience.build_experience_server
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: authenticated (`token_verifier` and `auth_settings` were already
  required and already reached the `FastMCP` constructor), but its
  `context_product` resource was entitlement-free and perspective-free exactly
  like the other two doors
- After: two further required keyword-only parameters — `entitlement_source`
  and `perspective_resolver`, imported from
  `ccf_runtime.authz.product_entitlement` and never re-declared here
- Why: this is the surface external agent runtimes reach; egress is the
  fabric-internal one. A fabric whose external door is less governed than its
  internal one has its threat model backwards, and this phase's founding
  complaint is *"an MCP server in front of a database"* — shipping the SDK's own
  front door ungated would be that complaint, self-inflicted. The seams are
  imported rather than re-declared because three doors with three readings of
  "entitled" is the drift `run_gates`/`run_federated_gates` share their
  comparison functions specifically to prevent
- Migration: authentication is unchanged; existing callers add the two
  governance seams on the same terms as the egress door above. The shared home
  is `ccf_runtime.authz.product_entitlement`, not a sibling MCP module: the two
  MCP roles may not import each other (`test_mcp_role_separation.py`), so the
  seams live in a package neither owns — the resolution
  `ccf_runtime.authz.protocol` already models for the two HITL doors. Worked
  example: `examples/external/00-hello-context/serve.py` with the `entitlement`
  block in `artifacts/experience.yaml`

*Recorded by `15.5-06-egress-entitlement.md`.*

#### ccf_runtime.http_api.routes.product.build_router

- Surface: ccf_runtime.http_api.routes.product.build_router
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: `build_router(deps)` — one GET route with no principal anywhere on it
- After: `build_router(deps, *, entitlement_source=None,
  perspective_resolver=None)`, and the route gains an optional `role` query
  parameter and 403 responses carrying the shared typed constants. Supplying
  exactly one of the two seams raises `ValueError`
- Why: the seams are optional *here* and required on the two MCP doors, and the
  asymmetry is deliberate: authentication on this surface is `create_app`'s
  `auth=` hook, which is itself optional by ruling (D-IMPL-73, the
  acknowledged insecure default), so a required seam would make a still-supported
  posture unbuildable. `create_app` warns instead. The role is a query
  parameter rather than a fourth path segment because the three path segments
  are the product's *address* and a role is the caller's request about capacity
- Migration: existing callers are unaffected — both parameters default to
  `None` and the unbound route is byte-identical in behaviour to the recorded
  T-07-24 posture. A deployment that wants delivery gated supplies **both**
  seams and binds `auth=`; supplying one alone is refused at build time, and
  supplying both without `auth=` emits `CcfDeadEntitlementWarning`

*Recorded by `15.5-06-egress-entitlement.md`.*

#### ccf.mcp.client.McpResourceClient

- Surface: ccf.mcp.client.McpResourceClient
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: `(*, url, bridge=None)` — no way to present a credential, so an
  authenticated MCP server could only be read by dropping to
  `run_with_session` and re-implementing the three operations this class
  already offers
- After: an optional `http_client_factory` parameter, threaded to
  `run_with_session` unchanged by all three async operations
- Why: the egress door is now authenticated, and every SDK MCP server is. The
  seam already existed one layer down (`run_with_session` has taken an
  `HttpClientFactory` since D-26); this exposes it on the class consumers

#### ccf.products.contract.RegisteredProductClass

- Surface: ccf.products.contract.RegisteredProductClass
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: eight fields — `schema_name`, `schema_version`, `ttl_anchor`,
  `assembly_mode`, `max_ttl_key`, `max_ttl_version`,
  `accepted_policy_binding_modes`, `accepted_lineage_modes`. Of the four §6.3
  elements the module docstring placed here, only `assembly_mode` existed
- After: six further fields, every one defaulted — `freshness_sla`,
  `discovery`, `addressability`, `constituent_validity_floors`,
  `payload_schema_key` and `payload_schema_version`. Between this class and
  `ContextProductContract` all nine §6.3 elements are now borne by named
  fields, asserted by `tests/products/test_contract_elements.py` with nothing
  pending
- Why: D-IMPL-106 (freshness), D-IMPL-98 (discovery and addressability, ruled
  *not* declaration-only), D-IMPL-31 (the floors) and D-IMPL-97 ruling 1 (the
  declared payload schema). Class-level throughout, because a product does not
  carry a copy of its class's governance — it is governed by it — and because
  that is the placement under which no recorded content address moves
- Migration: **nothing is required of an existing adopter.** Every new field
  defaults to a named positive sentinel, so a `register_product_class` call
  written before this plan constructs unchanged and the resulting class states
  what it always stated. To adopt: pass `freshness_sla=FreshnessSLA(...)` for
  the per-signal currency expectation; `discovery=ProductDiscovery(...)` to
  publish the class to a registry; `addressability=ProductAddress(...)` for the
  address it answers at; `constituent_validity_floors=...` to declare the
  D-IMPL-31 floors ahead of 15.5-12's refusal; and
  `payload_schema_key=` / `payload_schema_version=` to pin a declared payload
  schema, which must already be registered in the Control Plane

*Recorded by `15.5-07-contract-elements.md`.*

#### ccf.products.contract.register_product_class

- Surface: ccf.products.contract.register_product_class
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: eight keyword parameters; resolved and type-checked the class's
  MAX_TTL and nothing else
- After: six further keyword parameters carrying the fields above, all
  defaulted. When a payload-schema pin is declared, the schema is **resolved at
  registration** and refused — `ProductClassRegistrationError`, raised and
  naming both sides — if the pin is half-declared, names nothing registered, or
  names an artifact that is not a payload schema
- Why: D-IMPL-102 limb 1, *schema validity at registration*: a deployment that
  pinned a schema that is not there finds out while wiring the fabric rather
  than when a request is about to be bound to it, which is the MAX_TTL
  reasoning (D-IMPL-39) applied to the second piece of pinned governance. The
  well-formedness half is structural rather than a check that could be
  forgotten — a malformed schema cannot be constructed at all — so what remains
  for registration is that the pinned artifact *is* one
- Migration: none for an existing caller; every added parameter is
  keyword-only with a default. A caller adopting the payload schema registers
  the schema first and passes the `(key, version)` the registration minted.
  **No fourth gate follows**: `ccf.products.gates.run_gates` is byte-untouched
  and the three shipped validation gates stay at three (D-IMPL-102 limb 3)

*Recorded by `15.5-07-contract-elements.md`.*

- Surface: ccf.skills.catalog.SkillArgumentProperty

- Before: two required fields, `type` and `description`, and no way to describe
  anything below the top level
- After: three further fields, all defaulted to "not declared" — `properties`
  (an object-typed property's own members), `items` (an array-typed property's
  element spec) and `required` (which of its own members must be present).

  beneficial-owner list into parallel arrays preserves the values while
  degrading the pairing to an index convention the schema cannot state
- Migration: **none — this is a widening, not a replacement.** Every existing
  depth-1 property is still valid with the two fields it always had, and an
  unset nesting field is not a declaration: a leaf renders exactly the two keys
  it rendered before

#### ccf_runtime.mcp.egress.ProductResolverProtocol

- Surface: ccf_runtime.mcp.egress.ProductResolverProtocol
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: `__call__(*, tenant: str, product_class: str, version: str) -> ServableProduct`
- After:
  `__call__(*, tenant, product_class, version, perspective: Perspective, request: ProductRequest | None) -> ServableProduct`
- Why: D-IMPL-108, closing DI-15.5-03. The door resolves and authorizes a
  `Perspective` and must be able to hand it to the path that shapes the
  product, or the authorization is a refusal check and nothing more.
  **Neither new argument is defaulted, and `perspective` is not nullable** —
  that is the substance rather than a style choice. A resolver silently
  constructing its own perspective is indistinguishable from one honouring the
  door's, and a parameter defaulting to `None` would recreate exactly that
  ambiguity one layer down. `request` is required-with-no-default but typed
  `ProductRequest | None`, because a surface can honestly have **no way to
  ask**: the `ccf-product://` template is three path segments with no query
  among them, and manufacturing a subject, an intent, a freshness figure and
  an instant would be the SDK holding deployment values (CINV-01) and reading
  a clock — the literal-instead-of-argument defect D-IMPL-98 exists to remove,
  reintroduced one layer up. That is the same voice `requested_role: str | None`
  already carries on `PerspectiveResolverProtocol`.
  **Reclassified from `behavior` to `reshaped` by plan `15.6-10`**, under the
  authorization `D-IMPL-110` recorded by name and `D-IMPL-122` implemented.
  Editing a landed fragment is otherwise forbidden; this edit exists only
  because that ruling anticipated it. **The original `behavior` classification
  was correct when it was made** — `reshaped` fails
  `tests/test_surface_completeness.py` when the manifest shows no diff line to
  point at, and at the time it could show none: `inspect.signature` on a
  `Protocol` resolves `__init__`, so this seam's widening from three arguments
  to five was byte-invisible in `docs/surface/v0.2-surface.json`. `15.6-10`
  taught the tool to read a Protocol's `__call__`, the manifest now shows this
  name under `reshaped`, and the honest classification and the representable one
  have converged
- Migration: **required, and mechanical.** Every resolver a deployment supplies
  gains two keyword-only parameters. Eleven definitions across `runtime/`,
  `examples/` and `tests/` were updated in this plan's commits; an adopter's
  own is the same edit. The minimum conforming change is to accept both and
  ignore them, which type-checks and runs — but a resolver that ignores
  `perspective` is asserting *the conditioning this door authorized does not
  affect what I serve*, which is a claim worth making deliberately. The
  reference deployments do not: `examples/04-cross-process/producer_child.py`
  and `examples/external/00-hello-context/serve.py` both refuse to serve when
  the authorized perspective is not the one their product was assembled under

*Recorded by `15.5-15-resolver-seam.md`.*

  `subject`, `intent`, `freshness` and `asked_at` and carries no `role`, no
  `schema_name`, no `schema_version` and no `parameters`. The resource, the URI
  template and the resolver Protocol are untouched
- Change type: reshaped
- Why: `D-IMPL-126` item 5, gating HW-2 in `D-IMPL-127`. A resource-only door
  cannot refute the reading that a Context Product is a precalculated static
  object, because a caller with no way to ask a question cannot demonstrate that
  the answer depends on one. Opt-in rather than on-by-default because a
  deployment that reviewed and approved a resource-only door must not acquire a
  parameterised authorization surface it never assessed merely by upgrading —
  deny-by-default, this module's stated posture, applied to exposure. Two
  arguments rather than one because *is this door open?* must be answerable by
  grepping for a boolean. No `DEFAULT_*` description constant ships, unlike the
  Experience server's tools: the prose an adopter's consumers read is not the
  SDK's to write (CINV-01)
- Migration: **none required.** Every existing call site keeps working
  unchanged and registers no tool, which is the whole point of the default. To
  open the door, pass `expose_product_tool=True` **and**
  `product_tool_description="…"` together; see *Adopter migration* above,
  including the measured constraint that a class declaring any required request
  parameter is not reachable through the tool

*Recorded by `16-23-mcp-product-tool.md`.*

#### ccf_runtime.mcp.experience.build_experience_server

- Surface: ccf_runtime.mcp.experience.build_experience_server

- After: two additional keyword-only parameters, `entitled_product_class` and `lineage_tenant`, both `str | None = None` and both required conditionally on exposure — and refused when supplied for a tool the allowlist does not admit

A second entry for this name after `15.5-06-egress-entitlement.md` is deliberate: that fragment recorded the arrival of the governance seams, this one records the declared address the two now-gated tools are decided against

A deployment whose entitlement policy does not name the class its context provider serves will now be refused at its own front door — that is the gate working

#### ccf.client.adapters.binding_document.BindingDocument

- Surface: ccf.client.adapters.binding_document.BindingDocument
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: fifteen fields. A deployment could say where its config, its
  projection, its artifact store and its graph were, and could say nothing at
  all about the program a transport might have to launch to reach it
- After: a sixteenth field, `server: Path | None` — this deployment's own server
  program, resolved absolute against the directory **holding** the deployment
  and `None` when the document states none. Contained but deliberately **not**
  existence-checked: whether the program has to be on disk is the transport's
  question (`mcp+stdio` asks, because it launches it; an in-process deployment
  never does), and the `artifact_store` precedent rather than the `config` one
  is the right one
- Why: a deployment already declares how it is *assembled* — its projection, its
  Control Plane document, its graph. How it is *reached* is the same kind of
  fact and was the one thing a client had to be told out of band, in its own
  binding string. The base is the deployment root's **parent** rather than the
  root because a server program is not deployment content: the ordinary case is
  a remote server reached at an endpoint, with this key **absent entirely**, and
  a rule forcing the program inside the root would teach that a server belongs
  in a deployment, which is false
- Migration: none for a reader — the field is `None` on every document that does
  not declare one, and no existing document did. A deployment that wants to be
  reachable over `mcp+stdio` must now declare `server:`; see the adapter entry
  below

*Recorded by `18.1-04-the-deployment-declares-its-server.md`.*

  sentinel field, on the `GraphQuery.allowed_entities` precedent. `None` admits

  example-locally
- After: one added field, `defaults: Mapping[str, Any] =
  Field(default_factory=dict)` marked hash-transparent, with `_KEY_DEFAULTS =
  "defaults"` beside `_KEY_UNSUPPORTED_ARGUMENTS`. `from_declared` reads the
  optional **fifth** key when present and defaults to the empty mapping when
  absent, refusing a non-mapping in the same one-error voice the four other
  keys use. A `model_validator` refuses, **in one message naming every
  offender**, a default whose name is not a declared argument, a default for a
  name the class declares and always refuses, and a default whose value fails

- Why: `24.6-L-07`, `D-IMPL-253` Q2, Dave: *"Product defaults belong on the
  request contract. They define what omission means for that product."* A
  default applied from code could not be pinned, and a decision made under it
  could not be replayed — so omission has to mean something a deployment
  declared, resolvable to `(artifact, version)` and recorded with authority
  `default` (`ccf.products.provenance.EffectiveParameter`). The three refusals

#### ccf.products.request.ProductRequest

- Surface: ccf.products.request.ProductRequest
- Public surface: true

  hash-transparent at it

  carrying one is a different question** — it is content-addressed with the rest
  of the question, so two callers asking the same thing with and without an

  asking: the principal is still resolved at the door from a verified grant, and
  naming a policy establishes nothing on its own

  hashes exactly as it did — the empty tuple is omitted from the canonical form,

- Surface: ccf.products.request.ProductRequestContract

#### ccf.products.entitlement.ProductEntitlementGrant

- Surface: ccf.products.entitlement.ProductEntitlementGrant
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: two declared sets, `permitted_schema_names` and `permitted_roles`,
  neither with a default
- After: a third, `overridable_policies: frozenset[str]`, defaulted to the empty
  set and hash-transparent at it
- Why: `D-IMPL-253` Q7, Dave: *"The resolver must also establish that the
  caller/principal is entitled to exercise that override. Otherwise anyone who
  knows a policy ID could bypass it."* **It is not a bypass and could not become
  one**: an entry grants no class, no role and no subject, and the constraint
  artifact must itself declare `overridable` for the exception to exist — two
  declarations by two authors, and an override honored only where they agree.
  The default is the safe direction: an author who says nothing has granted
  nothing
- Migration: none required. Every entitlement policy already in force keeps its
  content address and its pin, and grants no override until one is declared

#### ccf.replay.record.PolicyBindingsSnapshot

- Surface: ccf.replay.record.PolicyBindingsSnapshot
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: five fields — the bindings, the HITL block, the survivor cap and the
  three adapter fields
- After: `request_resolution: str`, defaulted to `NO_REQUEST_RESOLUTION` and
  hash-transparent at it. At a real resolution it carries the canonical bytes of
  the `EffectiveRequest`, rendered from the value by the builder rather than
  accepted as a pre-serialized block, so one resolution cannot land as a family
  of blocks
- Why: `D-IMPL-253` Q1/Q6 and `D-IMPL-254`. The bindings in force at decision
  time now include *which constraint bounded which parameter, on whose
  authority, and whether an override was entitled*; the constraint versions are
  pinned beside it as `PolicyBinding` rows, so an examiner resolves the policy
  that was in force **then** rather than the one in force now
- Migration: none required. Every record written before this field keeps its
  content address — measured by `tests/replay/test_golden_13bd250.py`, not

#### ccf.products.resolver.GovernedResolver

- Surface: ccf.products.resolver.GovernedResolver
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: thirteen constructor arguments, none defaulted; `__call__` compared the
  raw request against the declared surface, then read the graph, then folded the
  class ceiling with `request.parameters["debt_tolerance"]`
- After: fifteen, still none defaulted — `constraint_resolver` and
  `capabilities` join. `__call__` now runs the ruled sequence: defaults applied,
  caller values overlaid, the policy constraints in force at `asked_at` resolved
  with provenance, the technical capabilities held against them, and only then
  the *effective* request checked. The engine answers the effective question
  while `RequestIdentity.parameters` and replay dimension 5 keep what the caller
  supplied; dimension 2 carries the resolution and the pins it was resolved from
- Why: `D-IMPL-253` Q8 and `D-IMPL-254` — this is the Authority layer's place in
  the sequence. A resolution after the read would have bounded a question the
  engine had already answered, and a default applied after validation would
  never have been the value the class declared
- Migration: a deployment constructing this class directly passes the two new
  arguments; `build_governed_resolver` supplies both. A conformity refusal now
  reaches the caller as `constraint-refusal`, `policy-resolution-conflict` or
  `product-request-violation`, all three carrying no lineage as before

#### ccf.products.resolver.build_governed_resolver

- Surface: ccf.products.resolver.build_governed_resolver

  `ReferencePolicyConstraintResolver` over the Control Plane this fabric booted
  against, keyed to the tenant's entitlement policy; `capabilities` defaults to
  what the booted fabric can be asked for, which is the empty tuple on every
  shipped boot path
- Why: the reference is selected here for the reason the debt scorer is —
  a deployment providing only data never has to know the Protocol exists. Unlike
  the scorer this default needs no material, so there is no second pair of

#### ccf.products.contract.ServeObligations.debt_ceiling → .default_debt_tolerance

- Surface: ccf.products.contract.ServeObligations
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: `debt_ceiling: Decimal | None` — the class's `D_c` ceiling. A request
  could only *tighten* it; a request could not create one; the declared-obligations
  gate refused an over-ceiling product by name, and the HTTP door answered `409`
- After: `default_debt_tolerance: Decimal | None` — the class's *declared
  default* tolerance, applied only when the caller states none, with authority
  `default` and the product-class artifact's pin as its source. No gate reads
  it. A caller's **looser** value is honored
- Why: `D-IMPL-251` C1=A, Dave: *"A product class cannot independently withhold
  otherwise deliverable context because its own debt preference was exceeded …
  The class value can be a declared/default tolerance characteristic, but it is
  not itself a policy boundary."* And `D-IMPL-253` Q9 on the name: *"Rename it."*
  — keeping the old name *"after changing its authority would perpetuate the
  conceptual error we just fixed."*
- Migration: an authored `ccf.product-class` document renames the key under
  `serve_obligations`. `extra=forbid` means the old key is refused at parse
  rather than silently ignored, which is the intended failure — a deployment
  that meant a ceiling has to decide whether it meant a default (leave it on the
  class), a caller-owned tolerance (declare the argument on the request contract)
  or governance (author a `ccf.policy-constraint`)
- Related: `docs/schemas/ccf.product-class.json` regenerated;
  `ProductClassDeclaration.serve_obligations`'s docstring follows

*Recorded by `24.6-04-the-default-tolerance-and-the-tolerance-exceeded-shell.md`.*

  RefusalEvidence | None = None`, `provenance: EffectiveRequest | None = None`,

  = None`. Every one is hash-transparent at its sentinel, so a shell that

#### ccf_runtime.mcp.experience.build_experience_server

- Surface: ccf_runtime.mcp.experience.build_experience_server
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: `build_experience_server(*, server_name, product_resolver, …,
  entitlement_source, perspective_resolver, entitled_product_class=None,
  lineage_tenant=None, tool_allowlist=None)`. A door could be stood up making
  governed entitlement determinations with no way to record any of them, and
  its denials raised through the transport.
- After: one additive keyword-only parameter, `refusal_recorder:
  RefusalRecorderProtocol | None = None`, placed after `perspective_resolver`.
  It is checked **first** — ahead of the allowlist and provider checks —
  through
  `ccf_runtime.authz.delivery_boundary::recorded_boundary`, which raises
  `UnrecordableDeliveryBoundaryError` for `None` and for a non-conforming
  object. The three entitlement paths now call
  `ccf_runtime.authz.delivery_boundary::govern_entitlement` and encode its
  return.

  determinations without the ability to record them is not a valid governed
  door."* This builder **always** entitles — the templated product resource is
  not allowlist-gated, so every server it produces makes governed
  determinations — which is why the requiredness is unconditional where every
  other D-03 requiredness on this builder is conditional on exposure, and why
  the check runs before them. The `None` default exists so the omission is
  refused by the one typed error rather than by a bare `TypeError` that would
  say nothing about why.

  recorder.** Pass `refusal_recorder=` a
  `ccf.products.resolver.RefusalRecorderProtocol` — the SDK ships
  `ReplayRefusalRecorder`, built over the artifact store the deployment's
  resolver already holds, so one deployment keeps one audit trail rather than
  two. A deployment that reaches the fabric through
  `ccf.products.resolver.build_governed_resolver` already has one at
  `resolver.refusal_recorder`. A door built without it does not answer at all,
  by construction — deliberately, so auditability is never contingent on
  outcome.

#### ccf.products.request.ArgumentDomain

- Surface: ccf.products.request.ArgumentDomain
- Public surface: true
- Change type: reshaped
- Before: numeric bounds only — `minimum: Decimal | None`, `maximum: Decimal | None`;
  refused at construction when neither end was named, an end was non-finite, or the ends
  were inverted; `refuses(value: Decimal)` named which end a number missed
- After: two shapes, exactly one of them. A third field `members: tuple[str | int | bool |
  Decimal, ...] | None` (hash-transparent at `None`) declares a closed member set over any
  supported primitive type — string, numeric (`int` and `Decimal` as one class), boolean
  (`bool` its own class, read first). Construction refuses, naming the defect: both shapes
  declared; neither shape; an empty set; a non-finite numeric member; a heterogeneous set;
  a duplicated member (duplication judged by the membership rule itself, so `1` and
  `Decimal("1")` are duplicates while `1` and `True` are a heterogeneous pair).
  `refuses(value: object)` is widened: the numeric shape judges magnitude as before; the
  enumerated shape judges exact typed equality — class first, then value under that class's
  own equality — and returns `not-in-domain` on a miss. Nothing trims, folds, aliases or
  substitutes
- Why: `D-IMPL-264` D-03/D-04/D-06 — the contract is the one declaration of record for a
  parameter's legal values (P-1), and cp-04 could not declare the legal values of a
  non-numeric parameter (`CP04-G-26`)
- Migration: none for existing declarations. A deployment declares
  `argument_domains: {<parameter>: {members: [...]}}` for a closed set, or keeps
  `{minimum: …, maximum: …}` for bounds — never both on one parameter. A caller of
  `refuses()` may now pass any value; a numeric domain answers `None` for a value with no
  magnitude, as the domain step always did

*Recorded by `24.7-01-the-request-contract-declares-an-enumerated-domain.md`.*
